ECON 630 · Fall 2026

Is there still a Phillips curve?

Testing the inflation–unemployment tradeoff in U.S. data, 1949–2026

Data: BLS via FRED: CPI (CPIAUCSL) and unemployment rate (UNRATE), monthly

The question

Does lower unemployment come with higher inflation, and has that tradeoff held steady over 75 years?

1 · Original curve

Inflation level vs. the unemployment rate. Phillips (1958); Samuelson & Solow (1960).

2 · Expectations-augmented

Change in inflation vs. unemployment. Friedman (1968) and Phelps (1967): only surprises trade off. Where Δinflation = 0 is the NAIRU.

3 · Stability over time

Estimate both versions separately in five monetary-policy eras and see whether the slope moves.

Data & method

931 months of CPI and unemployment, split into five eras

Inflation = year-over-year % change in CPI. Δinflation = change in that rate over 12 months. Each era is fit with simple OLS: y = a + b·unemployment. A Phillips curve means b < 0.

1949–1969
Early postwar
The era Phillips and Samuelson–Solow described
1970–1984
Great Inflation
Oil shocks, stagflation, the Volcker disinflation
1985–2007
Great Moderation
Low, stable inflation
2008–2019
Post-GFC
Deep recession, "missing disinflation"
2020–2026
Pandemic & after
14.8% unemployment, then the 2021–23 inflation surge

October 2025 is missing from both FRED series (BLS publication gap during the 2025 government shutdown) and is excluded.

The raw data

Inflation and unemployment sometimes move in opposite directions, and sometimes together

Finding 1

Over the full sample, there is no Phillips curve

+0.08
correlation of inflation and unemployment, 1949–2026 (monthly)
0.01
R² of the original curve. Unemployment explains essentially none of the variation in inflation.
Finding 2

The original curve held in 1949–1969, then broke down

  • 1949–69: each extra point of unemployment is associated with 0.9 pp lower inflation
  • 1970–2019: the slope is close to zero; unemployment explains ≤2% of inflation
  • 2020–26: the slope is negative again, driven by 2022
Finding 3

The 1970s support Friedman–Phelps: unemployment moved the change in inflation

  • 1970–84: slope -1.24, R² 0.43 (monthly), the best fit of any model
  • Implied NAIRU (dotted): 6.9% in 1970–84, falling to 5.4% in 1985–2007
  • Flat since 2008, consistent with anchored expectations
Finding 4

The tradeoff comes and goes over time

Each point is the correlation over the preceding 120 months. It turns positive when inflation and unemployment move together: stagflation in the 1970s, the late-1990s boom (both falling), and the 2020 shock.

Finding 5

Phillips loops: the curve shifts up as expectations rise, then back down

Left: inflation ratchets up through the 1970s at every unemployment level, and the Volcker disinflation brings inflation down only as unemployment nears 10% (1982). Right: the 2020 spike, then 8% inflation at 3.6% unemployment in 2022.

Caveats

What this simple test can't tell us

  • Headline CPI includes food and energy, so the supply shocks of 1973–74, 1979 and 2021–22 enter inflation directly. Core CPI would be cleaner.
  • No expectations data. Last year's inflation is a crude proxy for expected inflation, and a poorer one once expectations are anchored.
  • Overlapping 12-month changes are highly autocorrelated, so monthly N overstates the independent information. R² is descriptive only.
  • Simultaneity: the Fed raises rates when inflation is high, which raises unemployment. The OLS slope mixes the curve with the policy response.
  • Era cutoffs are chosen, not estimated, and the NAIRU is held constant within each era.
Conclusion

There is no stable, exploitable tradeoff

  • The original curve appears in 1949–1969 and briefly in 2020–2026, but not over the full sample.
  • The expectations-augmented curve fits best when expectations were moving (1970–1984) and fades once they are anchored (after 2008).
  • The 2021–23 surge fits a curve that steepens in very tight labor markets, but supply shocks could explain it just as well.

The data side with Friedman and Phelps: unemployment has traded off against surprise inflation, not a permanently higher level.
